questions.enonce_markdown: **(i)** In a certain city one car in four fails an inspection test. A sample of ten cars is selected at random from the city. Calculate, correct to four decimal places, the probability that at most two of the ten cars fail the inspection test.

**(ii)** Siri is a computer student who is learning how to type. The number of errors she makes per page follows a Poisson distribution with mean 3.

Calculate, to three decimal places, the probability that,

(a) the first page she types will contain exactly three errors.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $X$ be the number of errors on one page: $X \sim \text{Po}(3)$, with $P(X = r) = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}$ and $\lambda = 3$.

$$P(X = 3) = \frac{e^{-3} \times 3^3}{3!} = \frac{27\,e^{-3}}{6} = 4.5\,e^{-3} = 0.22404\ldots$$

**$P(X = 3) = 0.224$ (3 d.p.).**

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) there are at least three errors on the first three pages that she types.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The numbers of errors on separate pages are independent Poisson variables, so the total number $Y$ of errors on three pages is Poisson with mean $3 \times 3 = 9$: $Y \sim \text{Po}(9)$.

$$P(Y \ge 3) = 1 - P(Y \le 2) = 1 - e^{-9}\left(1 + 9 + \frac{9^2}{2!}\right) = 1 - 50.5\,e^{-9}$$

$$50.5\,e^{-9} = 50.5 \times 0.00012341 = 0.006232$$

$$P(Y \ge 3) = 1 - 0.006232 = 0.99377\ldots$$

**$P(Y \ge 3) = 0.994$ (3 d.p.).**
